tagline: A rebuilt mountain road past Olympic jumps, divided lakes and river hamlets.
intro: High Peaks Scenic Byway winds through Adirondack mountain passes, river valleys, forests and hamlets between Lake Placid and Northway Exit 30. NYSDOT identifies scenic, natural and recreational themes for this 30-mile state byway, highlighting Chapel Pond, Roaring Brook Falls and the Cascade Lakes. Leaving Lake Placid, Route 73 climbs to 2,000 feet before following a high ridge beside the Cascade Lakes, with Pitchoff Mountain directly northwest.

An 1810 state highway act incorporated an existing road between Westport and Saranac Lake through Keene. The first effort left a largely impassable highway; in 1812 the legislature acknowledged inadequate funding. In 1816 it appointed commissioners to rebuild from opposite ends and meet midway. Work finished by 1818 on the North West Bay Road. The older route bypassed Lake Placid village to the southwest. In 1994, New York signed the proposal for the High Peaks Scenic Byway into law, giving the modern corridor its scenic designation.

From Lake Placid, the drive passes the Olympic ski jumps before reaching the Cascade Lakes and descending into Keene. Route 73 then follows the East Branch of the Ausable south through Keene Valley, crossing Johns Brook. The numbered highway ends at US 9; the scenic byway continues on US 9 to Northway Exit 30.

moments.title: Lake Placid Olympic Ski Jumping Complex
moments.text: The Lake Placid Club’s first jump here used the hillside itself as a takeoff surface in 1920. A steel tower followed in 1927 and was raised in 1928 for the jump later used at the 1932 Winter Olympics. That tower was demolished in 1977 to make way for two new jumps for the 1980 Games. The concrete towers were poured continuously using a jacking system: fifteen days for the larger tower, nine for the smaller. A gondola replaced the aging double chairlift serving the ski jumps in 2019. Both jumps received further upgrades for year-round training in 2021.

moments.title: Cascade Mountain
moments.text: The Cascade Lakes began as one body of water, Long Pond, beneath a mountain then called Long Pond Mountain. A landslide shortly after 1860 split the pond in two. The divided waters were called Edmund’s Ponds until 1878, when Sidney and Warren Weston built a hotel between them. The Westons renamed them Cascade Lakes for the waterfall flowing down the landslide’s path; the mountain took the Cascade name as well. Route 73 passes both Upper and Lower Cascade Lakes with Pitchoff Mountain directly to the northwest. Cascade Mountain rises to 4,098 feet within the town of Keene in Essex County.
moments.notice: Upper and Lower Cascade Lakes lie beside Route 73, with Pitchoff Mountain to the northwest.

moments.title: Keene
moments.text: Keene’s bedrock lies close to the surface, leaving little land suitable for farming. Early development depended on lumber and iron extraction, but poor transportation meant most timber was used locally. A sawmill built in 1823 was followed by forges and gristmills. Keene Valley developed by 1840 under the name Keene Flats, which it kept until 1883. The town includes the separate hamlets of Keene, Keene Valley and St. Huberts, all along the East Branch of the Ausable River. Its boundaries contain fifteen of the 46 High Peaks, including Mount Marcy, and trailheads for many of those mountains.
